I used to ghostwrite SEO-optimized promotional web content for a living. I thought the good times would never end. Each morning, people I’d never met, flacks for various midsize B2B tech startups, would put in their orders. A Forbes editorial on improving business practices “during times of economic uncertainty.” A press release for a high-performance modular battery solution. A LinkedIn post, on the occasion of International Women’s Day, about the challenges faced by black women in STEM. I accepted each assignment with relish. I typed sentences like “In today’s unprecedented threat environment, air-gapped security isn’t a luxury—it’s a baseline necessity” with an impish smile on my face, convinced I was getting one over on the world. An insight like that, composed in under six seconds at a rate of $0.50 to $1.00 a word, could net me up to $14.00, depending on the client. An assortment of such insights, welded into more or less coherent texts in the six or seven weekly hours I allotted to this work, earned me roughly as much as a mid-career public school teacher, which was, from my perspective, more money than God: enough to buy any book I wanted, pay my share of the rent, and spend hours each day dreamily contemplating, if not exactly doing, the real writing around which I’d structured my life. The sheer absurdity of what I was up to—authoring thousands of words not to convey meaning to a human reader but to enhance the Google search ranking of various third-tier cybersecurity concerns—didn’t trouble me at all. That I could churn out corporate boilerplate so fluidly, and at such speed, seemed to me like a divine gift.

I don’t know if AI will ever be able to produce writing of value. But its ability to produce valueless writing was instantly evident, and so, from the moment of ChatGPT’s late 2022 launch, I knew it would ruin my life. My clients had always taken care with their briefs; they assembled the bullet points, I converted them into prose. Soon I was being sent transparently AI-generated outlines of a subtle, if frightening, illogicality, bureaucratic prose poems in which the same points were made and remade with slightly varying emphases across half a dozen subsections. I contemplated the fact that these outlines could in theory extend indefinitely—that a person could ask a machine to write a ten-thousand-page outline for an eight-hundred-word promotional article and that the machine would unhesitatingly comply. In this vision of infinitely compounding meaninglessness, I sensed something like true madness. Not that I intended to quibble: I wrote the articles as assigned. I knew that what these clients wanted from me was not sense per se but evidence of sufficient fealty to the whims of the waxing machine god, whose proclamations a startling percentage of the business world had instantly accepted as unassailable, the emanations of an objective ur-consciousness that one ignored at mortal peril. Within a year, my workload had dropped by half. Desperate, I cold-pitched my portfolio to hundreds of PR firms, my list of clips now prefaced by a rousing tribute to the value of human-authored prose in an environment increasingly flooded with the soulless output of machines. I didn’t buy a word of it; unfortunately, neither did they. For their purposes, ChatGPT would work just fine.

At this point, I was still managing to keep myself afloat, mostly through writing promotional copy about how AI would soon replace a range of once-viable professions, such as security guard, call center employee, and promotional copywriter. Why I was needed for this work at all was unclear to me; I chalked it up variously to pity, undepleted budgets drawn up pre-ChatGPT, or pure sadism.
